title: Before Pilate (John 18:28–19:16)
hookLine: Pilate asks what is truth and washes his hands

lines: OUT TO THE CROWD, BACK TO THE PRISONER.
cards: Early morning. Jesus is led to the headquarters of the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. In John, the council tells Pilate they have no power to put anyone to death.
That power is Rome's. What follows is almost a stage play. Pilate walks outside to the crowd, back inside to his prisoner, out again, in again.
Outside, voices getting louder. Inside, a quiet man in chains, and a governor who can't work out who he is.
And here's a strange thing: at Sunday Mass, in the Creed, Catholics say this man's name, a few words after the name of Mary. The old Apostles' Creed puts it: suffered under Pontius Pilate.

teach.h: MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.
teach.b: Pilate starts with the question that matters to Rome: are you a king? A king is a rival. Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "My kingdom is not of this world."

teach.h: WHAT IS TRUTH? HE DOESN'T WAIT.
teach.b: Jesus says he was born and came into the world to give testimony to the truth, and that everyone who is of the truth hears his voice. Then Pilate says the line: "What is truth?" And he doesn't wait.
John says he goes straight back out. A sneer? Tired?

An honest question? The text doesn't tell us his tone. Later readers found a wordplay in it: in Latin the question is quid est veritas, and shuffle those letters and you get est vir qui adest, it is the man who is here.
Nobody in the story says that. But it's the Christian answer: the truth was standing in front of him.

teach.h: NO FAULT IN HIM, AND HANDED OVER.
teach.b: Three times Pilate says he finds no fault in him. And still he hands him over to be crucified.
Matthew adds a picture: Pilate takes water and washes his hands in front of the crowd, as if that settled it.
It didn't. The hands were washed; the choice was still his. It was Rome that carried out the execution.
And the Catholic Church teaches plainly, at the Second Vatican Council and in its Catechism, that his death cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, or against the Jews of today.

how: Catholics hear John's account of the trial before Pilate every Good Friday, and they name Pilate each Sunday when they profess the Creed at Mass.

games.q: you're Pilate. you find no fault in this man, and the crowd outside is getting louder. what do you do?
o: set him free and face the crowd.
wash your hands and hand him over.
send him away to someone else's court.
games.why: he washes his hands in front of the crowd and hands Jesus over to be crucified. the water didn't make it someone else's choice.

practice: Think back over the last few weeks to a moment you knew something wasn't right and said, not my problem: a group chat that turned cruel, a coworker being talked about, a thing you could have said and didn't.
No need to punish yourself; just see it clearly, the way you'd see water running over your hands. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to answer the question Pilate walked away from.

wordCard.voice: Before Pilate. The Roman governor who asked what truth is, found no fault, and washed his hands anyway. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: truth. the word in Pilate's question, and in Jesus's answer just before it.

carryVoice: Your line: what is truth. That's Holy Week: palms, the tables, the perfume, the basin, the garden, the denials, and Pilate. See you tomorrow.
